newsitem.title: USA: Senate to start hearings on campaign funds scandal in July.
newsitem.headline: Senate to start hearings on campaign funds scandal in July.

text.p: The Republican chairman of the Senate committee investigating campaign fund-raising on Thursday accused Democrats of trying to delay his inquiry but said public hearings would begin the week of July 8.

Tennessee Sen. Fred Thompson, chairman of the Senate Governmental Affairs Committee, said "We will begin hearings the week of July 8 and they will be good hearings. We will begin to get answers to questions concerning whether or not the fundamental integrity of our government has been abused or compromised."
The committee was probing whether Asian business interests or the Chinese government tried to influence the 1996 presidential election by illegally donating funds to the Democratic Party.

The committee met to discuss Thompson's request to grant immunity from prosecution to 18 witnesses. But the seven Democrats on the committee vowed to oppose him. They have the power to block him since Thompson needed the votes of at least two Democrats to proceed with his plan.
Thompson unleashed a blistering attack on the Democrats, singling out Minority Leader Tom Daschle.
"We have seen a continuation, in fact an acceleration, of efforts by the minority under the apparent leadership of the minority leader, to delay the progress of this investigation," Thompson said.
Ohio Democratic Sen. John Glenn said Thompson was running a biased investigation.
"I don't see that we're having that fair, evenhanded investigation that Sen. Thompson promised," Glenn said.
He said he would not go along with granting immunity until the Justice Department gave assurances that doing so would not interfere with possible criminal proceedings.

The 18 witnesses to whom Thompson would like to grant immunity include several participants in a Democratic fund-raising event held in a Buddhist temple in California attended by Vice President Al Gore in April 1996.

The event may have violated the tax-exempt status of the religious institution and several individuals of modest means donated tens of thousands of dollars to the Democratic Party. Republicans suspect that the money was not theirs and hope that granting these witnesses immunity will persuade them to reveal where it came from.
